# How to Fact-Check a Suspicious Text or Link Before Forwarding It

> **In short:** Paste a suspicious message into any AI assistant to list its warning signs, then verify the claim yourself through a trusted channel. The AI cannot confirm that a link is safe or that a message is true, so treat its answer as a second pair of eyes.

A message that says "forward this to everyone now!" can make anyone hit send. This guide shows you how to use an AI assistant as a careful first reader: you'll build a reusable checklist, get a clear list of red flags, and finish with a plan for what to check before you share. It's written for anyone who already uses a chat assistant and wants a more reliable routine.

## Before you start
- An account on any AI assistant you already use. You know how to start a chat and send a message, so we skip that part.
- The suspicious text or link, copied into a notes app on your phone or computer.
- A free plan is usually enough for this. Very long pastes can be cut short on some plans, and limits can change, so check the reply is complete.
- About 10 minutes.

## Step 1 — Save a reusable checklist
Open your notes app and create a note called something like "Scam check template." Paste in the instructions below, so you never have to rewrite them. Most people find this helpful because the same checklist gets used every time, which keeps your review consistent.

Once saved, the template is simply copied into a new chat each time. You don't need any special settings or paid features for this; it's just a saved piece of text you control.

If your assistant has a feature for saved instructions or custom profiles, you can paste the template there instead. Look for a settings area with words like "instructions" or "custom." If you can't find one, the notes app works just as well.

💬 Example: "You are helping me check a message before I forward it. Look for these warning signs: urgency or pressure, requests for money, gift cards or passwords, a sender I can't verify, links that don't match the company they claim to be, and wording that feels off. Then list what you cannot tell from the text alone."

You'll know it worked when your note holds the full template and you can copy it in one tap.

## Step 2 — Start a fresh chat with the message
Open your AI assistant and start a new chat, so earlier conversations don't mix into this check. Copy the template from your note and paste it into the message box. Then add the suspicious message below it. Most assistants accept both in one message, and you should see your text appear in the chat box before you send.

Tell the assistant who sent it, if you know. That detail matters. If the message says it came from a friend, a bank, or a delivery company, mention that, but don't assume it's true.

If the box won't take a long paste, try pasting in two parts, with the template first and the message second in a new message. If the reply only covers part of the text, ask it to continue.

💬 Example: "Here is the message I received from [who sent it]: [paste the message here]"

You'll know it worked when the assistant replies with a structured list or a set of observations about the message, rather than just repeating your text back to you.

## Step 3 — Ask for the evidence behind each flag
A red flag is only useful if you know why it's there. Read the assistant's list, then send a follow-up asking it to show its reasons. This builds on the first answer, which is a simple but powerful way to get a more useful response.

Look for each flag to point to exact words from the message. If the assistant claims something is suspicious but can't point to a specific sentence, be skeptical of that flag and ask again.

If the follow-up answer is vague, rephrase your request with more specifics, such as "only list flags you can tie to a quoted sentence." Keep the chat open so the assistant remembers the message you pasted.

💬 Example: "For each warning sign you found, quote the exact words from the message and explain in one sentence why it could be a concern."

You'll know it worked when every flag comes with a quoted phrase and a short reason, so you can check the reasoning yourself in the original text.

## Step 4 — Inspect a link without tapping it
If the message contains a web address, don't tap it yet. Copy the address as text, or long-press it to copy, and paste it into the chat. The AI can break the address into parts so you can read it more clearly.

Here's what to look for. In an address like `https://usps-tracking.example.com/pay-now`, the name that matters most is the part right before the main ending, which here is `example.com`. The words in front of it can be anything, so a famous company's name at the start proves very little. The AI can help you spot that pattern, but it cannot visit the site to tell you whether it's live or dangerous.

Be cautious of shortened links and links that ask you to log in or pay right away. Those are reasons to slow down, not to panic.

💬 Example: "Break down this web address into its parts and tell me which part is the actual site name: [paste the address here]"

You'll know it worked when the assistant explains which part of the address belongs to the site and points out any mismatch with the company it claims to be.

## Step 5 — Confirm through a channel you trust
This is the most important step, and no AI can do it for you. Ask the assistant which claims in the message you would need to confirm directly. Then check each one through a source you already trust: type the company's address yourself, use the official app, or call the phone number printed on a bill or a card you own. Don't use a number or link that came inside the message.

If the message claims a friend is in trouble or needs money, call that person on a number you already have saved. Scammers often rely on urgency to stop people from checking.

If you can't reach anyone to confirm, the safe choice is to hold off on sharing it. Waiting costs almost nothing.

💬 Example: "Based on this message, what are the three most important claims I should confirm directly with the company before I share it?"

You'll know it worked when you have a short list of specific things to verify and a plan for how you'll check each one outside the message.

## Step 6 — Draft a calm heads-up for family
Once you know what you're going to do, ask the assistant to help you write a short message to the people you'd otherwise have forwarded to. A calm, specific note is more useful than an all-caps warning, and it helps your family learn the checking habit too.

Keep the draft short and kind. Mention what you found and what you're doing about it, without blaming the person who sent it to you. Read the draft before sending, because you know your family better than the assistant does.

💬 Example: "Write a short, calm message I can send to [family member name] saying I'm not sure this text is real, that we should check it with [trusted contact] first, and that they shouldn't share it yet."

You'll know it worked when you have a short, friendly draft that you can edit and send in your own voice.

## Common mistakes
- **Trusting the AI as the final judge.** The assistant reads the text you give it and can be wrong. The fix is to always confirm the key claims through a source you trust, as in Step 5.
- **Clicking the link to "see what it says."** Even a quick tap can load a page you didn't mean to visit. The fix is to paste the address into the chat as text, as in Step 4, and check it through the official site you type yourself.
- **Forwarding first and checking later.** Once a message is sent, you can't pull it back. The fix is to make Steps 2 to 5 a habit: pause, paste, check, then decide.

## What this means for you
- **In everyday life:** When a worrying text arrives about a package, a bill, or a relative in trouble, paste it into your checklist and follow the steps before anyone in your family acts on it.
- **For your business or work:** Keep the template in a shared note so coworkers can use the same checklist before forwarding a suspicious invoice or request to the team.
- **If you want to go further:** Try building a short library of templates for different situations, such as payment requests, delivery notices, or account alerts. Keep each one short, and test it on a message you already know is legitimate so you learn what a normal message looks like.

## Try it now
Open your notes app and save the template from Step 1. Then take one message you received recently, paste it into a new chat with the template, and read the first list of flags. You'll know this worked when you have a saved template and a short, quoted list of observations for a real message.
